analysis.one_liner: Phases out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers until they earn the full federal minimum.
analysis.headline: A bill to end the federal tipped minimum wage was introduced with 13 Democratic cosponsors and has sat without action in two House committees since September 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, employers can pay tipped workers as little as $2.13 an hour in cash and count customers' tips toward the rest of the federal minimum wage. This bill would raise that cash wage to $3.60 an hour immediately, then by $1.50 an hour each year until it reaches the full federal minimum wage, no matter how much an employee earns in tips. It would also bar employers and managers from keeping any portion of workers' tips, set up a process for employees to vote on tip-pooling systems, and require restaurants to disclose what happens to mandatory service charges.
analysis.who_benefits: Tipped workers, such as restaurant servers, bartenders, and hair stylists. Under current law their employer only has to make up the difference if tips fall short, and every hour they spend on nontipped work is paid at the reduced rate. The bill guarantees them at least the full federal minimum wage in cash wages, rising yearly, and guarantees they keep their tips, with penalties when employers or managers take any portion.

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces the tip credit, under which employers may pay tipped employees as little as $2.13 an hour in cash, with a schedule starting at $3.60 an hour and increasing by $1.50 an hour each year until it equals the full federal minimum wage under section 6(a)(1). [S2]

The bill states that any employee has the right to retain all tips they receive, and that an employer may not keep tips for any purpose other than distributing them through a lawful tip pool, including through managers and supervisors or to cover credit card transaction fees. [S2]

The bill lets non-supervisory employees trigger a vote on whether to create or change a tip-pooling system when 30% request it, with a 51% majority required to establish it, and bars employers from retaliating against workers over the vote or their participation. [S2]

The bill requires employers that add mandatory charges to a bill to disclose the reason and what portion goes to employees, to promptly pay over that portion, and to stop describing a charge as discretionary unless the customer requested it. [S2]

The bill tightens the definition of a tipped employee so that workers are no longer classified as tipped, and paid the reduced wage, during workweeks in which they spend more than 20% of their time on duties that do not earn tips. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Restaurants and other businesses that employ tipped workers, whose labor costs rise as the cash wage climbs toward the full minimum wage. Customers would likely see higher menu prices or more mandatory service charges, which the bill permits so long as the employer discloses them and passes the disclosed portion to employees.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the tip credit is a direct cost increase for restaurants, a sector that operates on thin margins, and opponents warn it could lead to job losses, reduced hours, faster adoption of ordering technology, and higher prices. [S2]

The bill's service-charge provisions effectively bless mandatory customer surcharges as a substitute for tips, provided employers disclose and pass along the employee-designated portion, so some diners could end up paying charges that feel like tips without the discretion a tip allows. [S2]

Workers whose tips already exceed the minimum wage would see no immediate pay increase, while their employers face higher costs, creating pressure to restructure pay or staffing in the highest-earning establishments. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers who earn little in tips, the guaranteed rising cash wage is a real, enforceable pay increase, and the tip-retention rules close loopholes where managers or processing fees eat into gratuities. The cost falls on restaurant owners and, through prices or surcharges, on customers. A fair reading is that this shifts income from business margins to low-paid workers, which is the bill's stated purpose; the strongest objection is about how restaurants absorb the cost, not about whether workers are better off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2025 and referred to the Education and Workforce and Ways and Means committees, where it has received no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote. The Congress does not end until January 2027, so it could still move, but nothing has happened to it so far.

narrative.text: Representative Jahana Hayes introduced the Tipped Worker Protection Act on September 3, 2025, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors. [S1]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce and, for parts within its jurisdiction, to the Committee on Ways and Means. [S4]
No further action appears in the bill's record after the initial referral; there are no committee votes, floor votes, or roll calls. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tipped workers gain nothing yet, because the bill has not advanced. Employers of tipped workers keep the status quo, paying the $2.13 tipped minimum as long as the bill sits without action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of tipped workers, for now

for.name: Rep. Jahana Hayes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 13 Democratic House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Adams, Ansari, Bonamici, Carson, Jackson (IL), Lee (PA), Lieu, Salinas, Thanedar, and Titus
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the bill sits in committees controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill ends the tip credit that lets restaurants pay tipped staff as little as $2.13 an hour in cash, directly raising labor costs. It softens the blow by allowing mandatory service charges to be passed to employees once disclosed, but the core effect is a wage transfer from restaurant margins to workers. [S2]

industries.industry: Payment card networks and card issuers
industries.note: The bill explicitly prohibits employers from covering debit or credit card transaction fees out of workers' tips, so card companies and merchants can no longer shift processing costs onto gratuity funds. [S2]

The bill imposes new recordkeeping duties on employers for tip-pool votes, tip retention, and service-charge disclosure, creating compliance work, while restricting certain tip-handling practices some platforms support. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: The bill has had no movement since its committee referrals in September 2025, and with only Democratic support in a Republican-led House, its usual path is to remain in committee without a hearing or markup. Its best realistic prospects are being folded into a larger wage or labor package, which is uncommon this late with a divided Congress.
